questions.prompt: Match each real node tier or tool from Chapter 1, Lesson 2 to what it actually stores or does.
right: A website that acts as the user interface for scraping a blockchain and looking up real transaction data, like EtherScan or Bitquery
Stores just enough data to connect to the network and broadcast transactions — a wallet app like MetaMask is a real example
Stores the most detail of any node tier — full historical, empirical transaction data, used for research or trading advantage
A standard network participant that stores more detail than a snapshot node, without going as far as an archive node
questions.explain: Snapshot/light nodes store just enough to connect and broadcast, like a wallet app. Full nodes store more detail than that. Archive nodes store the most detail of all — full historical data used for research or trading advantage. A block explorer isn't a node tier at all — it's the website front end, like EtherScan or Bitquery, that lets anyone look up ledger data. Lesson 2 tiers nodes this way specifically because of scalability: storing every last detail on every node everywhere would make the network far more expensive to run.

questions.prompt: What does a consensus algorithm actually do in a blockchain network, per Chapter 1, Lesson 4?
options: It determines the finality of transactions — how the network agrees, collectively, that a transaction actually happened and can't be undone
It encrypts transaction data so that only the sender and receiver can ever read it
It compresses block data so that more transactions fit inside each block
It assigns a permanent, unique hash to each wallet address so transactions can be tracked
It automatically converts a Proof of Work chain into a Proof of Stake chain once enough blocks have been mined
It determines which block explorer a given transaction is allowed to appear on
questions.explain: A consensus algorithm is what determines the finality of transactions sent on the blockchain — network-wide agreement that a transaction happened and can't be undone. Without one, the double-spend attack becomes possible: spending the same funds twice because the network never actually settled on what happened first.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes cryptography's job (Chapter 2), not consensus. Keeping data private from outsiders and getting the network to agree on transaction order and finality are two entirely different problems — a chain can have strong encryption and still be vulnerable to double-spending without a real consensus mechanism, and vice versa.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Proof of Work and Proof of Stake, per Chapter 1, Lesson 4.
options: Under Proof of Work, miners solve a random function, and the winner earns newly minted coins plus transaction fees
Under Proof of Stake, a validator's influence is determined by their computing power, not by how much they've staked
Under Proof of Stake, blocks are "verified" by validators rather than "produced" by a miner solving a function
A double-spend attack is only possible on a Proof of Stake chain, never on a Proof of Work chain
Flashbots/MEV involves bribing a block producer to get a transaction included in an advantageous position
questions.explain: Miners solve a random function and earn newly minted coins plus fees under Proof of Work — that's the real mechanism that produces blocks. Under Proof of Stake, validators verify and vote instead, weighted by how much ether they've staked, not their computing power — so the statement about computing power determining influence is backwards. Blocks are 'verified' under PoS rather than 'produced' the way PoW miners produce them. A double-spend attack is exactly the risk any weak consensus mechanism creates, regardless of whether it's PoW or PoS — it isn't unique to either. Flashbots/MEV is a real, documented dynamic: bribing a block producer for favorable transaction ordering.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in Chapter 1, Lesson 3's live hash demo, the specific hashing algorithm used was ________ — "secure hashing algorithm," 256 bits.
questions.explain: The live demo in Lesson 3 specifically named SHA-256 as the algorithm behind the hash generator — changing even one character of the input, like removing a period, produced a hash with nothing in common with the original.

questions.prompt: Per Chapter 1, Lesson 5, the class warns against one specific mistake when imagining blockchain's use in healthcare. What's the actual mistake being warned against?
options: Simply taking the idea of Bitcoin and putting it directly onto healthcare, instead of designing a system around the industry's real problem using blockchain's underlying properties
Assuming healthcare data can never legally be stored anywhere near a blockchain
Believing smart contracts are physically incapable of reading a diagnosis code
Assuming Bitcoin's transaction speed makes any healthcare use case technically impossible
questions.explain: Lesson 5's real warning is explicit: 'you wouldn't want to just take the idea of Bitcoin and put it on healthcare.' The actual lesson is to design a system suited to the industry's real problem — using blockchain's properties like decentralization and smart contracts — rather than copying Bitcoin's specific currency model onto an unrelated industry.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about digital signatures, per Chapter 2, Lesson 3.
options: A digital signature is created by encrypting a hash of the message using the sender's private key
Anyone holding the sender's public key can verify that signature
A digital signature proves non-repudiation — the sender can't later credibly deny having signed it
Encrypting a message for someone and signing a message both use the exact same key, in the exact same direction
Verifying a signature requires the signer's private key, not their public key
questions.explain: A digital signature is built by hashing a message, then encrypting that hash with the sender's private key. Anyone with the matching public key can verify it — confirming both who sent it (authentication) and that it hasn't been altered (integrity), plus non-repudiation, since only the sender holds the private key that produced it. Encrypting and signing are genuinely different directions: encrypting a message for someone uses the recipient's public key, while signing uses the sender's own private key — and verifying a signature uses the signer's public key, not their private key.

questions.prompt: A sender wants to send a message so that only the recipient can read it, and so the recipient can confirm it genuinely came from the sender. Per Chapter 2 and the PGP lesson in Chapter 3, which pair of keys does this actually require?
options: Encrypt the message with the recipient's public key; sign it with the sender's own private key
Encrypt the message with the sender's public key; sign it with the recipient's private key
Encrypt the message with the recipient's private key; sign it with the sender's public key
Use the sender's private key for both encrypting and signing
questions.explain: The PGP lesson makes this correction explicitly: encrypting a message uses the recipient's public key, so only the recipient's matching private key can decrypt it. Signing goes the opposite direction — it uses the sender's own private key, so anyone with the sender's public key can verify it. Mixing these two directions up is exactly the mistake the lesson calls out as an easy one to make.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a crypto system is called ________ when the sender and the receiver use the exact same key to both encrypt and decrypt data, as with AES or DES.
questions.explain: Symmetric cryptography means one shared key does both jobs — whoever holds that single key can lock and unlock the data. AES and DES are the two real algorithms named in Lesson 2 as symmetric systems, contrasted with RSA, the asymmetric example that uses separate public and private keys.

questions.prompt: Put these real, dated events from Bitcoin's history, per Chapter 3, in the correct chronological order.
items: Satoshi Nakamoto publishes the Bitcoin whitepaper (October 31, 2008)
The genesis block — block zero — is mined, embedding a Times newspaper headline (January 9, 2009)
The first real-world Bitcoin transaction takes place: 10,000 BTC for two pizzas, now celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day (2010)
Bitcoin reaches price parity with the US dollar (2011)
Bitcoin's price reaches an all-time high near $20,000 (2017)
questions.explain: The whitepaper came first (Oct 2008), followed roughly two months later by the genesis block (Jan 2009). The first real-world transaction — Bitcoin Pizza Day — didn't happen until 2010, well after the network was already running. Price parity with the dollar came in 2011, and the first major all-time high near $20,000 came in 2017 — each milestone building on the one before it, exactly as Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 lay them out.

questions.prompt: What is a Coinbase transaction, per Chapter 3?
options: The first transaction in a block, created by whoever mined that block, with no inputs, that mints new coins into circulation
A transaction fee paid to the Coinbase cryptocurrency exchange for processing a trade
The field in a block that records the hash of the block before it
A transaction that transfers an NFT from a seller to the winning bidder
A transaction a miner must sign using the entire network's shared private key before mining can begin
The transaction that moves ETH out of a smart contract's constructor into its first state variable
questions.explain: A Coinbase transaction is the first transaction in a block, created by whoever mined it. It's how new coins actually enter circulation — notably, it has no inputs, unlike a normal transaction that spends existing funds. Bitcoin's own genesis block Coinbase transaction minted the original 50 BTC reward.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is a tempting trap purely because of the shared name — Coinbase the cryptocurrency exchange has nothing to do with the Coinbase transaction, which is a protocol-level concept describing how a miner is rewarded with newly minted coins. The two share a name and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: after the fourth Bitcoin halving in April 2024, the mining reward dropped to ________ BTC — a quarter of the original 50 BTC genesis-era reward.
questions.explain: Bitcoin halving cuts the mining reward in half roughly every four years to enforce the 21 million coin hard cap. The very first block rewarded 50 BTC; after four halvings, the reward dropped to 3.125 BTC — exactly a quarter of the starting reward, as Lesson 5's milestone table lays out.

questions.prompt: Per Chapter 3, Lesson 3, why did e-gold ultimately fail despite genuine early popularity, especially with gold enthusiasts and early online traders?
options: It wasn't decentralized — a single company controlled it, so the U.S. government was able to shut the whole thing down
It ran out of physical gold reserves to back the currency it had issued
It used the same proof-of-work algorithm Bitcoin later used, which regulators made illegal shortly after
It simply never attracted enough users to stay financially viable
questions.explain: e-gold's one real, fatal weakness was centralization — a single company controlled it, which is exactly what let the U.S. government shut it down. That single fact is precisely the failure mode Bitcoin's decentralized design was built to avoid, as Lesson 3 draws out directly.

questions.prompt: Using Chapter 4's gas fee formula (gas fee = units of gas used x (base fee + priority fee)), a transaction uses 3 units of gas with a base fee of 10 gwei and a priority fee of 2 gwei. What is the total gas fee?
options: 36 gwei
15 gwei
30 gwei
12 gwei
questions.explain: 3 x (10 + 2) = 3 x 12 = 36 gwei — exactly the same formula worked through in class with 2 units of gas, an 11 gwei base fee, and a 3 gwei tip (2 x 14 = 28 gwei).

questions.prompt: Match each year (or date) to the real Ethereum milestone that happened then, per Chapter 4.
right: Ethereum's mainnet launches as "Frontier," its first public release aimed at developers
Vitalik Buterin publishes Ethereum's introductory whitepaper
The Merge joins Ethereum's execution layer with its new proof-of-stake consensus layer
Ethereum funds its own development through a 42-day public crowdsale (ICO)
questions.explain: Buterin's whitepaper came first, in 2013. Ethereum's own development was then funded in 2014 through a 42-day public ICO rather than traditional investors. Frontier, the first public mainnet release, launched in July 2015. Years later, on September 15, 2022, the Merge joined Ethereum's original execution layer with the Beacon Chain's proof-of-stake consensus layer.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the 2016 DAO hack and its aftermath, per Chapter 4, Lesson 4.
options: The DAO was drained of roughly 3.6 million ETH by an attacker exploiting a flaw in its code
Ethereum's developers used a hard fork to revert the chain's history and return the stolen funds
Ethereum Classic is the chain where the hack was reverted and the funds were restored, while Ethereum kept the original, unaltered history
Ethereum's growing popularity by late 2017, not the DAO hack itself, is what exposed the blockchain trilemma Buterin named
"The DAO" had raised roughly 150 million dollars' worth of Ether from over 11,000 investors before the attack
questions.explain: The DAO raised about $150 million in Ether from over 11,000 investors, then lost about 3.6 million ETH to an attacker's exploit. The community responded with a hard fork that reverted the chain and restored the stolen funds — that reverted chain became Ethereum, while Ethereum Classic is the original, unaltered chain that still includes the hack, kept alive by those who believed the chain's history shouldn't be changed even to undo a theft. That's the reverse of what the third option claims. Separately, it was Ethereum's own growing popularity by late 2017 — accelerated by CryptoKitties — that exposed the blockchain trilemma, not the 2016 DAO hack specifically.

questions.prompt: What is a constructor in Solidity, per Chapter 5?
options: A special function that runs exactly once, at the moment a contract is deployed, used to initialize its state
A function that must be called every single time a user interacts with the contract
The compiler step that converts Solidity source code into bytecode
A modifier that restricts a function so only the contract's owner can call it
A built-in Remix feature that automatically audits a contract for security vulnerabilities
The function responsible for converting bytecode back into readable Solidity source
questions.explain: A constructor runs exactly once — the moment a contract is deployed, and never again — and its real purpose is initializing the contract's state at that exact instant. In the Immutable contract example, the constructor sets both MY_ADDRESS (to msg.sender) and MY_UINT (to whatever value was supplied at deployment).
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an ordinary public function, which can be called any number of times after deployment — the entire point of a constructor is that it runs only once, at deployment, which is the opposite of 'every time a user interacts with the contract.'

questions.prompt: This loop runs i from 0 up toward 9. Based on what continue and break actually do, what happens at i = 3, and at what point does the loop actually stop running entirely?
options: At i = 3, continue skips the rest of that one iteration and jumps straight to i++; the loop then stops entirely once i reaches 5, because break exits immediately
The loop runs all the way through to i = 9, since continue later cancels out the effect of break
The loop stops entirely the moment i reaches 3, because continue halts the loop the same way break does
Having both continue and break in the same loop is a compiler error, so the loop never runs at all
questions.explain: continue skips only the rest of the current pass and moves on to the step (i++) — it does not stop the loop. break exits the loop entirely, immediately, the moment it runs. So at i = 3 the loop simply skips ahead to i = 4, and the loop actually terminates for good once i reaches 5.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a variable marked ________ can be set once, inside the constructor, and can never be modified again by any function for the rest of the contract's life.
questions.explain: immutable is exactly this kind of keyword — in the Immutable contract example, MY_ADDRESS and MY_UINT are both set once inside the constructor and locked forever after, which is genuinely useful for values like 'who deployed this contract' that should never change.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Solidity's data types and data locations, per Chapter 5.
options: storage is permanent and recorded on-chain, while memory is temporary and cleared after the function call ends
A uint can legally hold a negative value as long as it's wrapped in parentheses
uint is shorthand for uint256, but smaller sizes like uint8 exist and genuinely cost less gas to store
msg.sender is a global variable that always refers to whoever — or whatever — called the current function
calldata is a writable data location meant for a function's own internal temporary variables
questions.explain: storage is permanent and expensive, on-chain data; memory is temporary and cleared once the function call ends. uint really is shorthand for uint256, but smaller sizes exist specifically because a smaller size costs less gas to store when you know the value will stay small. msg.sender always refers to whoever called the current function — demonstrated live by switching accounts and watching owner change to match. A uint genuinely cannot hold a negative value under any circumstance — Remix flags it immediately with a red underline. And calldata is read-only, typically for external function inputs, not a writable location for internal temporary variables.

questions.prompt: Put the real lifecycle a Solidity contract goes through, per Chapter 5, in the correct order.
items: Write the contract in human-readable Solidity code
Compile it, converting the readable code into EVM-executable bytecode
Deploy the compiled bytecode to a blockchain, giving it a real contract address
Interact with it — calling its functions, now that it's actually live
questions.explain: Every contract in this course follows this exact real order: write the Solidity, compile it down to bytecode the EVM can run, deploy that bytecode to get a live contract address, and only then can anyone — including you — actually call its functions.

questions.prompt: In Chapter 5's SimpleStorage contract, Remix estimates calling set(5) at roughly 22,514 gas, versus just 2,453 gas for calling get(). Why is set so much more expensive?
options: set writes to a state variable, which requires an actual transaction that validators process and permanently record, while get only reads state and costs far less
get() is written using a more gas-efficient programming language than set()
set() always runs a hidden loop internally, while get() never does
Gas cost in Solidity depends only on a function's name length, not on whether it reads or writes state
questions.explain: The real, concrete rule from this chapter: writing to state costs real gas and requires sending a transaction, because it permanently changes what every node stores. Reading state with a view function like get() costs far less and doesn't require a transaction at all when called externally as a pure read — exactly the roughly 9x difference Remix showed side by side.

questions.prompt: In Remix, a contract's first line reads `pragma solidity 0.8.30;`, but the Solidity Compiler tab is still set to version 0.8.27. What happens when you try to compile it?
options: Remix flags a real compiler error that the source file requires a different compiler version; selecting the matching version (0.8.30) makes the error disappear
Remix automatically upgrades its own compiler setting to match the pragma, and the contract compiles without any warning
The contract compiles successfully anyway, since pragma only affects deployment, never compilation
Remix silently ignores the pragma line and always compiles with whichever version was installed first
questions.explain: This exact mismatch was demonstrated live in class: setting the pragma to 0.8.30 while the compiler was set to 0.8.27 produced the real error 'source file requires different compiler version.' Selecting the matching 0.8.30 compiler version made the error disappear, and the compile then succeeded.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Solidity itself, per Chapter 5, Lessons 1-2.
options: Solidity is described as "contract-oriented" because its entire design centers on writing and deploying smart contracts
Low-level languages like assembly give more direct hardware control, but are more error-prone than high-level languages
Solidity was created by Vitalik Buterin in 2014
A readable (view) function costs zero gas, while a writable function costs gas because it changes blockchain state
Remix, Foundry, and Hardhat all ultimately compile Solidity down to the same EVM bytecode target
questions.explain: Solidity is genuinely contract-oriented — its whole design centers on smart contracts. Low-level languages trade safety and ease for raw hardware control, which is exactly why they're more error-prone. A readable function costs zero gas while a writable one costs gas, because only the writable one actually changes state. And no matter which tool you use — Remix, Foundry, or Hardhat — the real destination is the same EVM bytecode. The one false statement: Solidity was created in 2014 by Gavin Wood, not Vitalik Buterin — Wood was also an Ethereum co-founder and later created Polkadot.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the EVM's stack holds up to 1,024 items, each 256 bits wide, and works as a ________-In-First-Out structure — the same real idea as a stack of plates, where you can only take from, or add to, the top.
questions.explain: The EVM's stack is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) structure. The class's own physical analogy was a stack of plates: you can only remove the top plate, and you can only add a new one to the top — pull from the middle, and everything above it falls, exactly like trying to access a value that isn't on top of the EVM's stack.

questions.prompt: A contract needs to list every address that has ever held a token balance. Per Chapter 6, Lesson 1, why can't a plain mapping alone do this?
options: A mapping only stores values, not a list of its own keys — Solidity gives no way to loop through a mapping's keys directly
Mappings can only ever hold a maximum of 256 keys at once
Looping through a mapping is so gas-expensive that Solidity forbids it at compile time
A mapping's keys are stored in a random order, so looping through them would return results out of sequence
questions.explain: Lesson 1 states this directly: mappings do not store keys, only values — Solidity doesn't keep a list of every key that's ever been set. If a contract needs to enumerate every address that's held a balance, it needs a separate array tracking those keys alongside the mapping, exactly the gap Lesson 2's arrays are introduced to fill.

questions.prompt: Match each ERC-20 interface function to what it actually does, per Chapter 6, Lesson 8.
right: Checks how much a spender is still allowed to spend on an owner's behalf
Sends tokens on someone else's behalf, once that spending has been approved
Returns the total number of tokens in existence
Lets another address spend a set amount of your own tokens
Returns how many tokens a specific wallet currently holds
questions.explain: totalSupply returns the total number of tokens that exist. balanceOf returns one wallet's holdings. approve lets another address spend a set amount of your tokens. allowance checks how much of that approval a spender still has left. transferFrom actually moves tokens on someone else's behalf, once approved — exactly the six-function IERC20 interface from Lesson 8, minus transfer itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the real differences between ERC-20 and ERC-721, per Chapter 6.
options: Every ERC-20 token is identical to every other, while every ERC-721 token has its own unique tokenId
ERC-721 tracks ownership with a mapping from tokenId to owner, while ERC-20 only ever needed a mapping from address to a plain balance amount
ERC-20 is the standard used for NFTs, while ERC-721 is the standard used for fungible currencies
OpenZeppelin provides an audited, importable ERC20 contract that a token can inherit from using `is ERC20`
A duplicate tokenId is allowed in ERC-721, as long as the two tokens are owned by two different addresses
questions.explain: ERC-20 tokens are fungible — identical and interchangeable — while every ERC-721 token has its own unique tokenId, which is exactly backwards from the claim about ERC-20 being used for NFTs. That's also why ERC-721 needs a mapping keyed by tokenId rather than just an amount per address. OpenZeppelin's ERC20.sol really can be inherited directly with `is ERC20`. And a duplicate tokenId is a hard, real rule violation in ERC-721 — `require(_owners[tokenId] == address(0), "Token already exists")` blocks it regardless of who's attempting to claim it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when new tokens are created by _mint, the Transfer event fires with ________ as the "from" address, since the tokens didn't move from any existing account — they simply came into existence.
questions.explain: Minting increases both the recipient's balance and totalSupply — new tokens are being created, not moved from somewhere else. That's exactly why the Transfer event uses address(0) as the 'from' address: there genuinely is no real sender, since the tokens didn't exist a moment before. Burning is the inverse case, using address(0) as the 'to' address instead.

questions.prompt: A contract has five different functions that should only ever be callable by its owner. Per Chapter 6, Lesson 5, what's the real problem with writing `require(msg.sender == owner, ...)` directly inside each of the five functions, instead of using a modifier?
options: The same check ends up duplicated five times, so any future change to the access-control logic has to be made in five separate places instead of just one
Solidity doesn't allow the exact same require statement to appear in more than one function in a contract
A require statement written inside a function body costs more gas than the identical check written inside a modifier
Without a modifier, msg.sender simply can't be compared against another address at all
questions.explain: The real, practical reason modifiers exist is to avoid copy-pasting the same check into every function that needs it. onlyOwner keeps that logic in exactly one place — change it once, and every function using the modifier picks up the change automatically, instead of needing five separate edits.

questions.prompt: Put these real steps of Chapter 6's token transfer function in the order they actually execute.
items: require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount, "Insufficient funds") checks the sender actually has enough balance
balances[msg.sender] -= amount; subtracts the amount from the sender
balances[to] += amount; adds the amount to the receiver
emit Transfer(msg.sender, to, amount); announces that the transfer happened
questions.explain: The require check runs first — if the sender doesn't have enough, the whole transaction reverts immediately and none of the balance changes below it ever happen. Only after that check passes does the function subtract from the sender, add to the receiver, and finally emit the Transfer event, announcing the change only after the state has actually been updated.

questions.prompt: A contract uses `mapping(address => Person) public directory;`, and every function reads or writes `directory[msg.sender]`. What does keying the mapping by msg.sender actually guarantee, per Chapter 6, Lesson 4?
options: Every account automatically gets its own, separate record — nobody can accidentally read or overwrite another account's data
Only the contract's original deployer can ever read any account's record
Every account shares exactly one Person record, which gets overwritten by whoever calls the function last
The struct's fields become publicly readable by anyone without needing to call a function at all
questions.explain: This was demonstrated live with two different accounts: calling addPerson from one account stored one record, switching to a different account and calling it again stored a completely separate record — and calling getMyInfo() from each account only ever returned that account's own data. Using msg.sender as the key is exactly what guarantees that separation automatically.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about events in Solidity, per Chapter 6, Lesson 6.
options: Events are cheaper to store than state variables, and are read-only — a contract can never read its own past events back
The indexed keyword can be applied to up to three parameters on one event, making them searchable and filterable in logs
Firing an event with emit automatically changes a contract's state variables
Front-end apps can listen for events to update in real time, instead of constantly polling a contract's state
An event must be declared inside a function body — it can't be declared at the contract level
questions.explain: Events log data cheaply and are read-only from the contract's own perspective. Up to three parameters per event can be marked indexed for fast, filterable searching. Front ends genuinely rely on listening for events instead of constantly re-checking state, exactly as the class's illustrative JavaScript snippet showed. Firing emit doesn't change any state variable itself — it's purely an announcement, separate from whatever state change (if any) happened just before it — and an event is declared at the contract level, the same place state variables are, not inside a function body.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ERC-20 is a standard for ________ tokens — every unit is identical and interchangeable with every other unit, like dollars or Bitcoin.
questions.explain: ERC-20 tokens are fungible — each one is exactly the same as every other, the way one dollar bill is interchangeable with any other dollar bill. That's the real contrast Lesson 13 draws with ERC-721, where every token is unique and carries its own tokenId.

questions.prompt: Per Chapter 7, which of these is a real, concrete difference between a Solidity library and a contract?
options: A library can't declare state variables or receive Ether, while a contract can do both
A library can be deployed to Ethereum's mainnet, but a contract can only ever run on a test network
Every function in a contract must be pure or view, while a library's functions can be any kind
Only a library can emit events — a contract is never allowed to
questions.explain: The real, concrete table from this lesson: libraries don't allow state variables, don't support inheritance, and can never transfer Ether — a contract can do all three. Libraries are meant to be a stateless toolbox of reusable (usually pure or view) functions, kept separate from full application logic, which is exactly what a contract is for.

questions.prompt: In Chapter 8's EtherWallet contract, `owner` is declared `address payable` instead of a plain `address`. Why does that matter?
options: Solidity's .transfer() function can only be called on an address marked payable, and withdraw() needs to send ETH to owner
A plain address can never be assigned a value inside a constructor
Every variable marked public is required to also be payable
It has no real effect — payable and address are fully interchangeable in Solidity
questions.explain: withdraw() calls payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount) — and Solidity only allows .transfer() on an address payable, not a plain address. That's exactly why owner is declared address payable public owner, and why msg.sender gets explicitly cast with payable(...) inside the constructor.

questions.prompt: Match each real modifier from Chapter 8's MultiSigWallet contract to what it actually checks.
right: Reverts if the given transaction index doesn't actually exist yet
Reverts if msg.sender isn't one of the wallet's registered owners
Reverts if this specific owner has already confirmed this exact transaction
Reverts if the transaction has already been executed
questions.explain: onlyOwner guards against callers who aren't registered owners at all. txExists guards against referencing a transaction index that was never actually submitted. notExecuted guards against re-running a transaction that already finished. notConfirmed guards against the same owner confirming the same transaction twice — four separate, necessary guard rails before any approval or execution is allowed to happen.

questions.prompt: In Chapter 8's English auction contract, why does start() call nft.transferFrom() to move the NFT into the auction contract itself, rather than just recording who the seller is?
options: The contract needs to actually hold the NFT in escrow so it can transfer it to the winning bidder once the auction ends
transferFrom is a required call that every Solidity constructor must make before it can finish running
Holding the NFT lets the auction contract mint additional copies of it while bidding is open
It's purely cosmetic — the NFT could just as easily stay in the seller's wallet for the whole auction
questions.explain: The auction contract doesn't create the NFT — it references an existing one through the IERC721 interface and manages bidding for it. Since the contract needs to actually be able to hand the NFT to the winning bidder once the auction ends, start() moves the token out of the seller's wallet and into the contract's own custody the moment the auction begins.

questions.prompt: In Chapter 10's vulnerable EtherStore contract, `balances[msg.sender] = 0` runs after the ETH is already sent via `.call`. If an attacker's fallback function calls withdraw() again before that first call ever finishes, what actually happens?
options: The balance check still passes, since balances[msg.sender] hasn't been reset yet, letting the attacker withdraw against the same balance repeatedly
The second withdraw() call automatically fails, because Solidity blocks a function from being called twice inside the same transaction
The attacker's fallback function never actually fires, since EtherStore only recognizes calls named deposit() or withdraw()
The contract detects the repeated call and reverts the entire transaction, including the original withdrawal
questions.explain: This is the exact, live exploit from Lesson 2: because the balance reset happens on the very last line, after the ETH has already been sent, the require(bal > 0) check in a re-entered withdraw() call still passes — the real balance was never actually zeroed out yet. That's how the class's Attack contract walked away with three ETH after depositing only one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the two real fixes for reentrancy covered in Chapter 10, Lesson 3.
options: Checks-effects-interactions means verifying conditions first, then updating state, then making external calls — in that order
A reentrancy guard modifier like noReentrant uses a boolean lock so that only one guarded call can be executing at a time
Reordering a function to follow checks-effects-interactions and adding a reentrancy guard are mutually exclusive — a contract can only ever use one of the two
Real production contracts typically write their own reentrancy guard from scratch rather than using OpenZeppelin's
A fallback function fires automatically when a contract receives ETH with no matching function call, which is the real mechanism a reentrancy attack hijacks
questions.explain: Checks-effects-interactions and a reentrancy guard are explicitly independent defenses — the lesson states a contract could use either one alone and still be protected from the exact exploit in the previous lesson, so they're not mutually exclusive. The guard pattern locks a boolean while a function runs, blocking any re-entered call from passing its own require check. And the fallback function is the real mechanism a reentrancy attack hijacks, firing automatically whenever ETH arrives with no matching function call. In production, the lesson's own honest note is that popular projects use OpenZeppelin's audited guard rather than writing their own from scratch.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the real pattern that fixes this class of bug runs in exactly this order — ________, effects, interactions.
questions.explain: Checks-effects-interactions means: first you do checks (like require(bal > 0)), then you make state changes or effects (like resetting a balance to zero), and only then do you perform external interactions, like sending Ether or calling another contract. Reordering the vulnerable withdraw() function to follow exactly this sequence is the real, one-line-reorder fix from Lesson 3.
